examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det+Head:D{form=demonstrative} This]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:NP#np [Det:D the] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP#adjp [Head:Adj{form=superlative} oldest]] [Head:N house] [Mod:PP#set [Head:Prep in] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N street]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Oldest is the superlative of old. The comparison is with the other members of a set, here the houses in the street, and the superlative picks out the one at the top of the scale. The PP in the street delimits the set.

examples.text: Kim is the younger of the two.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:NP#np [Det:D the] [Mod+Head:Adj#younger{form=comparative} younger] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep of] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Mod+Head:D{form=cardinal numeral} two]]]]]]
examples.explanation: With a set of two, careful usage has the comparative where a larger set would have the superlative (the youngest of the two is common informally). Younger is a fused modifier-head: it modifies an understood noun and heads the NP at once. Of the two names the set.

examples.text: Kim has the same bike as Pat.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V has] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D the] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj same]] [Head:N bike]] [Comp:PP#pp{cx=comparative complement (indirect: licensed by same)} [Head:Prep as] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Same expresses identity, not degree, so this is a non-scalar comparison. The as-phrase is licensed by same, which is a modifier inside the NP, so like the than-phrase after more it is an indirect complement, attached to the whole NP.

examples.text: Your plan is different from mine.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:NP{form=genitive; subject-determiner} [Head:N{form=pronoun, genitive} Your]] [Head:N plan]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:AdjP#adjp [Head:Adj different] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep from] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=pronoun, independent genitive} mine]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Different expresses non-scalar inequality. Its complement here is a from-phrase; than and to also occur after different, varying with region and register. Different is not a comparative form, and the PP is an ordinary complement of the adjective.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V sings] [Adjunct:PP#pp{cx=comparison of likeness} [Head:Prep like] [Comp:NP [Det:NP{form=genitive; subject-determiner} [Head:N{form=pronoun, genitive} her]] [Head:N mother]]]]]
examples.explanation: Like is a preposition here, with the NP her mother as its complement; the PP is a manner adjunct comparing Kim's singing with her mother's. Like can also take a finite clause (Kim sings like her mother did), a use that some style guides avoid in formal writing.

examples.context: Said by someone standing at a table, pointing at a chair across the room.
examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=imperative clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=plain form} Bring] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D#that{form=demonstrative; deictic, distal} that] [Head:N chair]] [Comp:PP#here [Head:Prep{form=deictic, proximal} here]]]]
examples.explanation: Three things are fixed by the situation. The addressee is understood as the subject of the imperative. That chair is picked out by pointing and by being away from the speaker (that, not this). Here means the speaker's location. Here is a preposition without a complement, a goal complement of bring.

examples.context: In a conversation, just after the speaker has explained a plan.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#i [Head:N{form=personal pronoun, 1st person singular, nominative} I]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V told] [Oi:NP#you [Head:N{form=personal pronoun, 2nd person, accusative} you]] [Od:NP#this [Det+Head:D{form=demonstrative} this]]]]
examples.explanation: I and you are deictic: they refer to whoever is speaking and whoever is addressed, so the same sentence names different people in different mouths. This points to something in the conversation, the plan just explained, rather than to something in the room.

examples.text: Pat lives in Leeds, and Kim works there.
examples.tree: [Coordination{cx=coordination of clauses} [Coord:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V lives] [Comp:PP#inleeds [Head:Prep in] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Leeds]]]]] [Coord:Clause [Marker:Crd and] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V works] [Adjunct:PP#there{ante=inleeds} [Head:Prep{form=anaphoric} there]]]]]]
examples.explanation: There is anaphoric here: it stands for a place already mentioned, and its antecedent is in Leeds. Like here, there is a preposition without a complement, so this anaphor is not a pronoun and its antecedent is not an NP.

examples.text: Kim said that she was tired.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#kim [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V said] [Comp:Clause{cx=declarative content clause} [Marker:Sbr that] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP#she{ante=kim} [Head:N{form=personal pronoun, 3rd person singular, nominative} she]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj tired]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: On the most natural reading she is an anaphor with Kim as its antecedent: it is interpreted as the same person. The link is a matter of interpretation, not of constituent structure, so it is recorded as a separate link rather than a branch. She could also refer to someone mentioned earlier in the conversation.

examples.text: Before she left, Kim locked the door.
examples.tree: [Clause [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep Before] [Comp:Clause [Subject:NP#she{ante=kim} [Head:N{form=personal pronoun, nominative} she]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left]]]] [Subject:NP#kim [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V locked] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N door]]]]
examples.explanation: She comes before its antecedent Kim, yet the link is natural, because she is inside the fronted adjunct before she left. An anaphor that precedes its antecedent is anticipatory. Before is a preposition taking a clause as its complement.

examples.text: She locked the door before Kim left.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#she [Head:N{form=personal pronoun, nominative} She]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V locked] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N door]] [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep before] [Comp:Clause [Subject:NP#kim [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Here she cannot refer to Kim: she is the subject of the main clause, and Kim is inside a dependent of that same clause. With these two NPs in this structural relation the anaphoric link is ruled out, so no antecedent is recorded; she must be someone else.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#kim [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V blamed] [Object:NP#refl{ante=kim} [Head:N{form=reflexive pronoun} herself]]]]
examples.explanation: Herself is the object, and its antecedent is the subject Kim. In complement function a reflexive is required when the object refers to the same person as the subject: Kim blamed her means someone else.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#kim [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V blamed] [Object:NP#obj [Head:N{form=personal pronoun, accusative} her]]]]
examples.explanation: With the ordinary pronoun her, the object cannot refer to Kim; it must be someone else, identified from the context. Reflexive and non-reflexive pronouns divide the work between them, so no antecedent link inside the sentence is recorded.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#kim [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V fixed] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N fence]] [Adjunct:NP#refl{ante=kim|cx=emphatic reflexive} [Head:N{form=reflexive pronoun} herself]]]]
examples.explanation: This herself is emphatic, not a complement: it can be left out (Kim fixed the fence), and it adds the sense of without help. It is shown as an adjunct in the VP, still linked to its antecedent Kim.

examples.context: Pat has just suggested taking the train.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#np [Det+Head:D#that{form=demonstrative; anaphoric} That]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:NP [Det:D a] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj good]] [Head:N idea]]]]]
examples.explanation: That refers back to Pat's suggestion: an anaphoric use of a demonstrative. Its antecedent is a stretch of the previous conversation, not an expression in this sentence, so no link is drawn. Standing alone, the determinative is a fused determiner-head of its NP.

examples.text: These boxes are heavier than those.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D#these{form=demonstrative, plural, proximal} These] [Head:N boxes]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V are] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj{form=comparative} heavier] [Comp:PP [Head:Prep than] [Comp:NP#those [Det+Head:D{form=demonstrative, plural, distal} those]]]]]]
examples.explanation: These and those agree in number with the noun (these boxes, not this boxes) and contrast in distance from the speaker. Those, without a noun, is a fused determiner-head, understood as those boxes.

examples.text: Kim wants a red bike, and Pat wants a blue one.
examples.tree: [Coordination{cx=coordination of clauses} [Coord:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V wants] [Object:NP [Det:D a] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj red]] [Head:N#bike bike]]]]] [Coord:Clause [Marker:Crd and] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V wants] [Object:NP#np [Det:D a] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj blue]] [Head:N#one{form=pro-nominal one|ante=bike} one]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: One stands for bike, not for a red bike: Pat wants a blue bike. Its antecedent is just the noun bike, without the determiner or the modifier, so pro-nominal one replaces part of an NP, not a whole NP, and takes its own determiner and modifier (a blue one).

examples.context: Asked whether the shop will be open on Sunday.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V thinks] [Comp:AdvP#so [Head:Adv{form=anaphoric so, standing for a clause} so]]]]
examples.explanation: So stands for a whole clause, the shop will be open on Sunday, taken from the question. It is the complement of thinks, in place of a content clause. The negative counterpart is not (Kim thinks not), though Kim doesn't think so is more usual.

examples.usage: As in: The lamps were on.
examples.tree: [N#w{form=plural} [Base:N#base lamp] [Affix:Suffix#sfx{form=plural suffix} s]]
examples.explanation: Lamps is a form of the lexeme lamp: the plural, made by adding the suffix ·s to the lexical base lamp. Inflection makes the forms of a single lexeme, so lamp and lamps share one dictionary entry; the suffix does not create a new word in that sense.

examples.usage: As in: Kim walked home.
examples.tree: [V#w{form=preterite} [Base:V#base walk] [Affix:Suffix#sfx{form=preterite suffix} ed]]
examples.explanation: Walked is the preterite of walk: the base plus the suffix ·ed. The same suffix makes the past participle (Kim has walked), so for regular verbs the two forms are spelled alike and are told apart by the constructions they occur in.

examples.usage: As in: Two geese landed on the pond.
examples.tree: [N#w{form=plural|cx=plural made by changing the vowel (no suffix)} [Base:N#base{form=base of goose with its vowel changed} geese]]
examples.explanation: Geese is the plural of goose, but no suffix is added: the operation changes the vowel of the base. The form cannot be divided into a base and a plural part, so the structure has a single piece, and the operation that produced it is named on the word.

examples.usage: As in: The bus is stopping.
examples.tree: [V#w{form=gerund-participle} [Base:V#base{base=stop|alt=doubling} stopp] [Affix:Suffix{form=gerund-participle suffix} ing]]
examples.explanation: The base stop is written stopp before ·ing: a single final consonant after a single stressed vowel doubles. The doubling keeps the spelling of the short vowel (compare hoping, from hope, with a long one).

examples.usage: As in: We are hoping for sun.
examples.tree: [V#w{form=gerund-participle} [Base:V#base{base=hope|alt=e-deletion} hop] [Affix:Suffix{form=gerund-participle suffix} ing]]
examples.explanation: The silent e of hope is dropped before a suffix beginning with a vowel: hope plus ·ing gives hoping. Before a consonant it stays (hopeful, hopeless).

examples.usage: As in: Pat carries the bags.
examples.tree: [V#w{form=3rd person singular present tense} [Base:V#base{base=carry|alt=y-replacement} carri] [Affix:Suffix{form=present tense suffix, spelled es after i} es]]
examples.explanation: A final y after a consonant becomes i before most suffixes (carry, carries, carried), and the suffix is then spelled ·es. Before ·ing the y stays (carrying), which avoids writing two i's together.

examples.usage: As in: Kim seems happier.
examples.tree: [Adj#w{form=comparative} [Base:Adj#base{base=happy|alt=y-replacement} happi] [Affix:Suffix#sfx{form=comparative suffix} er]]
examples.explanation: Happier is the comparative of happy: the base plus ·er, with y written i. Two-syllable adjectives ending in y take the suffix readily; many other two-syllable adjectives, and longer ones, use more instead (more careful).

examples.usage: As in: the biggest room
examples.tree: [Adj#w{form=superlative} [Base:Adj#base{base=big|alt=doubling} bigg] [Affix:Suffix#sfx{form=superlative suffix} est]]
examples.explanation: Biggest is the superlative: the base plus ·est, with the final g doubled. Grade is inflectional, so big, bigger and biggest are forms of one lexeme, while more and most are separate words in syntax.

examples.usage: As in: Put the knives away.
examples.tree: [N#w{form=plural} [Base:N#base{form=base of knife, modified: f becomes v} kniv] [Affix:Suffix{form=plural suffix} es]]
examples.explanation: Knives is irregular in a small way: the suffix is the regular one, but the base is modified, its final f sound becoming v. Compare the fully regular chiefs, where the base does not change.

examples.usage: As in: The sheep are in the field.
examples.tree: [N#w{form=plural|cx=base plural (same as the singular)} [Base:N#base sheep]]
examples.explanation: Here the plural form is the same as the singular. That it is plural shows only in agreement (the sheep are) and in determinatives (these sheep). A base plural is still an inflected form, just one with no visible change.

examples.usage: As in: Passers-by stopped to help.
examples.tree: [N#w{form=plural|cx=compound noun with the plural inside} [Base:N#first{form=plural} [Base:N#passer passer] [Affix:Suffix#sfx{form=plural suffix} s]] [Base:Prep#by by]]

marks.name: hyphen
marks.use: joins the two bases of the compound

examples.explanation: The plural suffix goes on the first base, passer, which carries the noun meaning of the compound: passers-by, not passer-bys (which is heard informally). The plural inflection attaches to that noun, wherever it stands in the compound.

examples.usage: As in: Have you eaten?
examples.tree: [V#w{form=past participle} [Base:V#base eat] [Affix:Suffix#sfx{form=past participle suffix} en]]
examples.explanation: Eaten is the past participle of eat, made with the suffix ·en, not ·ed. Its preterite ate is made differently again, by a change of vowel, so for this verb the preterite and past participle are different forms.

examples.usage: As in: We ate early.
examples.tree: [V#w{form=preterite|cx=preterite made by changing the vowel (no suffix)} [Base:V#base{form=base of eat with its vowel changed} ate]]
examples.explanation: Ate has no suffix: the preterite is made by changing the vowel of the base. Irregular verbs fall into classes by the operations they use; eat uses a vowel change for the preterite and ·en for the past participle.

examples.usage: As in: Isn't Kim ready?
examples.tree: [V#w{form=negative present tense} [Base:V#base{form=positive present tense form is} is] [Affix:Suffix#sfx{form=negative suffix} n't]]
examples.explanation: Isn't is a single word: the negative present-tense form of be, built from is with the negative suffix ·n't. Inversion shows it is one word: Isn't Kim ready? moves isn't as a whole, while the order with a separate not is Is Kim not ready?

examples.usage: As in: The door won't open.
examples.tree: [V#w{form=negative present tense|cx=irregular negative form of will} [Base:V#base won't]]
examples.explanation: Won't cannot be divided into will plus a negative suffix: the base itself changes. Irregular negative forms like won't and shan't show that these are stored inflected forms, not the output of a regular contraction rule.

examples.usage: As in: Their unhappiness was obvious.
examples.tree: [N#w [Base:Adj#unhappy{form=derived adjective} [Affix:Prefix#un{form=negative prefix} un] [Base:Adj#happy{base=happy|alt=y-replacement} happi]] [Affix:Suffix#ness{form=noun-forming suffix} ness]]
examples.explanation: The structure has two layers. First the prefix un· attaches to the adjective happy, giving the adjective unhappy; then ·ness attaches to that, making a noun. The other bracketing is unlikely because negative un· attaches freely to adjectives (unkind, unwise) but hardly at all to nouns.

examples.usage: As in: a rewritable disc
examples.tree: [Adj#w [Base:V#rewrite [Affix:Prefix{form=prefix meaning again} re] [Base:V#write{base=write|alt=e-deletion} writ]] [Affix:Suffix#able{form=adjective-forming suffix} able]]
examples.explanation: Re· attaches to the verb write, making the verb rewrite; ·able then turns that verb into an adjective meaning able to be rewritten. The e of write drops before ·able.

examples.usage: As in: Thank you for your kindness.
examples.tree: [N#w [Base:Adj#base kind] [Affix:Suffix#sfx{form=noun-forming suffix} ness]]
examples.explanation: ·ness turns the adjective kind into the noun kindness, a new lexeme with forms of its own (kindnesses). The suffix decides the category of the result: whatever the base, a word in ·ness is a noun.

examples.usage: Also spelled modernize. As in: They plan to modernise the station.
examples.tree: [V#w [Base:Adj#base modern] [Affix:Suffix#sfx{form=verb-forming suffix} ise]]
examples.explanation: ·ise (also spelled ·ize) makes verbs from adjectives and nouns: modernise means make modern. The result is a verb with its own inflected forms (modernised, modernising).

examples.usage: As in: That was unkind.
examples.tree: [Adj#w [Affix:Prefix#pfx{form=negative prefix} un] [Base:Adj#base kind]]
examples.explanation: Prefixes usually change the meaning but not the category: unkind is an adjective, like kind. In English it is mostly suffixes that change the category of the base.

examples.usage: As in: A blackbird sang.
examples.tree: [N#w{cx=compound noun} [Base:Adj#black black] [Base:N#bird bird]]
examples.explanation: Blackbird is one word made of two bases, the adjective black and the noun bird. It names a species: a blackbird is a kind of bird, and the right-hand base bird makes the whole a noun. Its main stress falls on black, as in other compound nouns.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#np [Det:D A] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP#adjp [Head:Adj black]] [Head:N bird]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V landed]]]
examples.explanation: Here black and bird are separate words: an adjective phrase modifying a noun inside an NP. Any bird that is black qualifies, and black can be modified (a very black bird), which is impossible inside the compound (*a very blackbird).

examples.usage: As in: The bookshelf is full.
examples.tree: [N#w{cx=compound noun} [Base:N#book book] [Base:N#shelf shelf]]
examples.explanation: Two nouns: the second, shelf, is the centre of the compound, and the first narrows it down, a shelf for books. Noun plus noun is the most productive compound pattern in English.

examples.usage: As a verb, in: We bottle the cider in May.
examples.tree: [V#w{cx=conversion from the noun bottle} [Base:N#base bottle]]
examples.explanation: The verb bottle (put into bottles) is made from the noun bottle without any affix. It is a verb because it behaves as one: it takes verb inflections (bottled, bottling) and heads a VP.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=pronoun} We]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=preterite; converted from the noun bottle} bottled] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N cider]]]]
examples.explanation: In a sentence the converted verb shows its new category: it has the preterite inflection ·ed and takes an object, the cider. Nothing in the base marks the conversion; only this behaviour does.

examples.usage: As a noun, in: We went for a walk.
examples.tree: [N#w{cx=conversion from the verb walk} [Base:V#base walk]]
examples.explanation: Conversion also runs the other way: the verb walk gives a noun walk, which takes a determiner and a plural (two walks). The two lexemes share a form but belong to different categories.

examples.usage: As in: She works in a lab.
examples.tree: [N#w{cx=clipping of laboratory} [Base:N#base{form=what remains of laboratory} lab]]
examples.explanation: Lab is a clipping: part of laboratory used as a word on its own, with the same meaning in a more informal style. Clipping removes material instead of adding it.

examples.usage: As in: We met for brunch.
examples.tree: [N#w{cx=blend of breakfast and lunch} [Base:Splinter#br{form=from breakfast} br] [Base:Splinter#unch{form=from lunch} unch]]
examples.explanation: Brunch is a blend: the start of breakfast fused with the end of lunch, for a meal that replaces both. Its parts are splinters, pieces of words that are neither affixes nor bases elsewhere.

examples.usage: As in: Pat will edit the report.
examples.tree: [V#w{cx=back-formation from the noun editor} [Base:V#base{form=editor without what looked like a suffix} edit]]
examples.explanation: The noun editor came first; the verb edit was made by removing what looked like the agent suffix ·or, as if editor were edit plus ·or. Back-formation runs against the usual direction of derivation.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=declarative clause} [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left] [Adjunct:AdvP [Head:Adv early]]]]

marks.name: full stop
marks.use: ends the sentence and presents it as a statement

examples.explanation: The full stop closes the sentence and marks it as complete. For a declarative clause used to make a statement it is the default terminal.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=declarative clause (used as a question)} [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left] [Adjunct:AdvP [Head:Adv early]]]]

marks.name: question mark
marks.use: ends the sentence and presents it as a question

examples.explanation: The same declarative clause, but the question mark shows it is being asked, not stated: a declarative question, typically checking or expressing surprise. The terminal signals the kind of speech act; the clause is still declarative, with no inversion.

examples.tree: [Coordination#co{cx=coordination of main clauses without a coordinator} [Coord:Clause#c1 [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V cooked]]] [Coord:Clause#c2 [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V washed] [Comp:PP [Head:Prep up]]]]]

marks.name: semicolon
marks.use: separates two main clauses joined without a coordinator

marks.name: full stop
marks.use: ends the sentence

examples.explanation: Two main clauses are joined without a coordinator, and the semicolon marks the boundary between them. A comma alone here would be what style guides call a comma splice; a full stop, or a comma with and, would also do.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause [Subject:Coordination#co{cx=coordination of NPs} [Coord:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Coord:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Coord:NP [Marker:Crd and] [Head:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Sam]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V arrived]]]

marks.name: comma
marks.use: separates two coordinates where no coordinator is written

marks.name: full stop
marks.use: ends the sentence

examples.explanation: In a list of three coordinates only the last has a coordinator; the comma marks the boundary between the first two. A comma before and as well (Kim, Pat, and Sam) is a matter of house style, the serial comma.

examples.text: Kim had one aim: to win.
examples.tree: [Clause#clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V had] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D one] [Head:N aim]]] [Supplement:Clause#sup{cx=supplement spelling out what precedes|anchor=obj} [Predicate:VP [Marker:Sbr to] [Head:VP [Predicator:V{form=plain form} win]]]]]

marks.name: colon
marks.use: introduces a supplement that spells out what precedes

marks.name: full stop
marks.use: ends the sentence, and with it the supplement

examples.explanation: The colon introduces an elaboration: to win spells out what the one aim is. It marks the start of the supplement, whose anchor is the NP one aim. The supplement ends where the sentence ends, so the full stop closes both.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause [Subject:NP#subj [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Supplement:NP#sup{cx=appositive supplement|anchor=subj} [Det:D a] [Head:N nurse]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V resigned]]]

marks.name: opening parenthesis
marks.use: opens a supplement set apart as an aside

marks.name: closing parenthesis
marks.use: closes the supplement

marks.name: full stop
marks.use: ends the sentence

examples.explanation: Parentheses do the same structural job as the commas in Kim, my neighbour, fixed the fence, but set the supplement further apart, as an aside. Unlike commas and dashes, parentheses always come in pairs, even at the end of a sentence.

examples.usage: Putting the full stop after the closing quotation mark, as here, is usual in British practice; American practice puts it inside.
examples.tree: [Clause#clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V called] [Object:NP [Head:N{form=pronoun} it]] [PredComp:NP#pc [Det:D a] [Head:N disaster]]]]

marks.name: opening quotation mark
marks.use: opens words presented as someone else's

marks.name: closing quotation mark
marks.use: closes the quoted words

marks.name: full stop
marks.use: ends the sentence

examples.explanation: The quotation marks show that a disaster is Kim's wording, not the writer's. Grammatically nothing changes: the NP is still the predicative complement of called, and the marks sit exactly at its boundaries.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V called] [Object:NP [Head:N{form=pronoun} it]] [PredComp:NP#pc [Det:D a] [Head:N disaster]]]]
examples.explanation: Without quotation marks the writer takes responsibility for the description. The structure is the same as with them: it is the object, and a disaster is a predicative complement describing it.

examples.usage: Before a noun, as in: a well-known writer
examples.tree: [Adj#w{cx=compound adjective} [Base:Adv#well well] [Base:Adj#known{form=past participle used as an adjective} known]]

marks.name: hyphen
marks.use: joins the two bases of a compound adjective

examples.explanation: Before a noun, well and known are joined by a hyphen and treated here as one word, a compound adjective. The hyphen marks a boundary between the two bases inside the word, not a boundary between constituents of a sentence.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N writer]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:AdjP#adjp [Mod:AdvP [Head:Adv well]] [Head:Adj known]]]]
examples.explanation: After the verb, the same words are usually written without a hyphen: well is an adverb phrase modifying the adjective known in an ordinary AdjP. The hyphen appears where the words are used as a single word before a noun.

contrasts.explanation: Both are the NP the new teacher, so the category is identical. In the first it is the subject (before the verb, the verb agrees with it); in the second it is the object of met. Function is a relation to the containing clause, not a property of the phrase.

Both follow the verb and both are NPs. The object of met denotes a second participant and can be the subject of a passive. The predicative complement of became describes Kim, has no passive, and alternates with an AdjP (Kim became famous).
Same function, different category: each is a predicative complement, but one is an NP and the other an AdjP. A label like 'predicative adjective' merges two independent questions.
Both are locative PPs at the end of the VP. On the shelf is required by put and so is a complement; on the train is optional with slept and could combine with almost any verb, so it is an adjunct.
The identical PP in Leeds is a complement of lives (Pat lives is incomplete in this sense) but an adjunct with met. Whether a dependent is a complement depends on the head it combines with.
On Monday is predicative complement of be in the first (the clause needs it) and an optional time adjunct in the second.
Pat is the recipient in both, but only in the first is it an indirect object. In the second the recipient is expressed by the PP to Pat, a complement of a different category and function.
Enough is a determinative in both. In enough money it is the determiner of an NP; in big enough it is a post-head modifier in an AdjP. Determinative is the category, determiner the function.
Three is a determinative in both. Alone it is the determiner; after the, which takes the determiner function, it becomes a modifier within the nominal.

Calm is an adjective phrase describing Kim, as predicative complement of sounded. Calmly is an adverb phrase describing the manner of speaking, as an adjunct. The choice follows from function: sound takes a predicative complement, speak takes a manner adjunct.

Singing is a verb in the first (modified by an adverb, heading a clause) and a noun in the second (with a determiner, heading an NP). The tests are about dependents: adverbs and objects go with verbs, determiners and adjectives with nouns.

The same words, what Pat cooked, are an NP in the first (the thing Pat cooked, which Kim ate) and an interrogative clause in the second (the question which thing Pat cooked). Paraphrases show the difference: the thing that Pat cooked fits only the first; which thing Pat cooked only the second.
Both follow claim and begin with that. The relative clause has a gap (made what? the claim) and modifies the noun; the content clause is complete and expresses the claim's content as a complement.
That is a meaningless, often omissible marker of a content clause. Because carries meaning, cannot be omitted and heads a PP whose complement is the clause.

Kim is the agent in both sentences, but only in the active is it the subject. In the passive the subject is the window and Kim is the complement of by. Subject is a syntactic function; agent is a semantic role.

In the coordination both Kim and Pat are coordinates of the subject, which counts as plural. In the supplement, my neighbour adds information about Kim but is not part of the subject; the subject is just Kim.
Who won the prize identifies which student and is integrated into the NP as a modifier. Who lives in Leeds adds information about a sister already identified; it is a supplement, set off by commas.
In looked up the word, up is a one-word PP and the word is the verb's object; the particle can move (looked the word up). In looked up the chimney, up the chimney is one PP and cannot be split.

The words are identical. In the first reading in the tree is inside the object NP, modifying bird; in the second it is an adjunct in the VP. Ambiguity of this kind is ambiguity of constituent structure.
Has is an auxiliary in the perfect, taking a past-participial clause complement; it is a lexical verb of possession taking an NP object in the second.
Outside is a preposition in both: intransitive in the first, transitive with the house as complement in the second, much as a verb may occur with or without an object.
The content clause is an extraposed subject in the first, with dummy it as the subject; in the second it is itself the subject. Meaning is the same; information packaging differs.
Happy is an adjective in both. Attributively it modifies the head child inside the NP; predicatively it is the complement of be. These are the two central functions of adjectives.

Both say something negative about Kim. Only the first is a negative clause: its tag is is she? In the second the negation is part of the adjective unhappy, and the clause takes isn't she?, like any positive clause.

In both, not is an adverb. After the finite auxiliary has it marks primary verbal negation, and the whole clause is negative. Before to know it negates only that non-finite clause; the main clause stays positive.

Both contain the negative determinative no in a phrase after the verb. In the first the negation reaches the clause (tag: did she?). In the second it stays inside the PP in no time, which means quickly, and the clause is positive (tag: didn't she?).

Two frequency adjuncts in the same position. Rarely makes the clause negative (does she?); often leaves it positive (doesn't she?). Approximate negators count as negative even though they assert a small amount, not zero.

The same words in a different order. Before didn't, deliberately has wider scope than the negation: Kim chose not to answer. After it, inside the complement clause, the negation has wider scope: it is false that Kim answered deliberately.
Both are determinatives in determiner function. Any needs a non-affirmative context, here the negative clause; some is positively oriented and natural in the positive clause.

Both compare heights on one scale. Taller than states inequality; as tall as states equality. The governor differs (the comparative inflection versus the degree adverb as), and so does the head of the complement (than versus as).

In both, than heads a comparative complement. In the first the governor is the comparative inflection of the head, taller. In the second the governor is the determiner more while the head is books: the complement is licensed by a dependent.
Than takes an NP in the first and a reduced clause in the second, with the same meaning. In the clause the missing degree element is shown as a gap; with the NP Pat nothing is shown as missing.

Both are comparisons of inequality. Tall takes the inflection, so the governor is part of the word taller. Careful does not, so the governor is the separate determinative more, which modifies the adjective.
Both pick out one member of a set. With more than two members the superlative oldest is used; with exactly two, careful usage prefers the comparative younger.

Both comparisons are non-scalar: no degrees are compared. Same expresses identity and licenses an as-phrase from inside the NP; different expresses a difference and takes its own complement, here from mine.
Here gets its reference from the speech situation, the speaker's location. There gets it from an antecedent in the text, in Leeds: an anaphoric use of a word that can also be deictic.

In both, she comes before Kim. In the first she is inside a fronted adjunct and can take Kim as its antecedent. In the second she is the main-clause subject and Kim is inside a dependent of that clause, and the link is impossible.
The same position, the object of blamed. The reflexive herself must take the subject Kim as its antecedent; the personal pronoun her must not.
Both are herself with Kim as antecedent. As the object of blamed it is a complement and cannot be left out. In the second it is emphatic, an optional adjunct meaning roughly without help.

Both leave a noun to be understood from earlier. With one, a pro-form heads the nominal (a blue one); without it, the adjective blue fuses with the head (the blue). The determiner matters: a blue alone is not used this way, while the blue is.
Both are plural forms of nouns. Lamps is made by suffixation and splits into base and suffix; geese is made by changing the base and has no separate plural piece.
Both express comparative grade. Happier does it inside the word, with a suffix; more careful does it in syntax, with the determinative more modifying the adjective.
Both are plurals. Lamps shows it with a suffix; sheep shows nothing in its form, so its plural is visible only through agreement and determinatives.
Both are preterites. Walked is regular, the base plus ·ed. Ate has no suffix; the change of vowel is the whole operation.
Isn't is one word, the negative form of be. In the second, not is a separate word, an adverb after the auxiliary. Both give primary verbal negation; only the first is inflectional.
Both add a suffix to a base. ·ness is derivational: it makes a new lexeme of a different category. ·s is inflectional: it makes a form of the same lexeme lamp.
The same two items. As a compound, blackbird is one noun naming a species, stressed on black. As a phrase, black bird is an NP in which the adjective modifies the noun and can itself be modified.
Both are conversions without an affix. Bottle goes from noun to verb, walk from verb to noun; the only evidence of the new category is how each word inflects and combines.
The words and the clause structure are identical. The full stop presents the clause as a statement; the question mark presents the same declarative clause as a question.

In the first the supplement sits mid-sentence, so a second comma closes it. In the second the supplement ends the sentence, and the full stop does both jobs: it ends the sentence and closes the supplement.
The structure is identical: a disaster is the predicative complement in both. The quotation marks attribute the wording to Kim; without them the writer takes it on.
The same two words. Before a noun they form a hyphenated compound adjective, one word. After be they are two words in an AdjP, and the hyphen is normally dropped.
